positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter views safe implementation of generative AI-enabled devices as a shared human responsibility that cannot rest on any single party, and emphasizes that oversight roles must span the full AI lifecycle rather than a single regulatory stage.
positions.requested_fda_action: FDA should recognize governance and oversight involving a broad set of stakeholders—including patients and caregivers, nurses, physicians, pharmacists, informaticians, engineers, developers, cybersecurity/IT, human-factors, quality and safety, ethics, regulatory, administrative, educational, and research personnel, and manufacturers—engaged from design and validation through implementation, monitoring, reassessment, and retirement, with clearly defined accountability and meaningful human oversight.

gap_explanations.distributed_accountability: The comment frames safety as a shared responsibility across many professional roles and calls for clearly defined accountability among them, which extends beyond FDA's manufacturer-centered framing.
gap_explanations.deployment_assurance_scalability: It extends oversight roles to implementation, monitoring, reassessment, and retirement at the point of care, not just premarket or manufacturer-run postmarket activities.
gap_explanations.human_ai_system_performance: The comment ties safe use to meaningful human oversight and the involvement of human-factors and usability experts throughout the lifecycle.

positions.public_summary: Comment supports multi-stakeholder governance of generative AI-enabled devices but broadens FDA's postmarket framing: patients, clinicians, informaticians, engineers, cybersecurity, human-factors, ethics, quality, and administrative personnel, plus manufacturers, should be engaged from design through retirement, with clearly defined accountability and meaningful human oversight.
positions.source_passage: Regulation of generative AI-enabled medical devices must recognize that safe implementation is a shared human responsibility. Governance and oversight should include patients and caregivers; nurses; physicians; pharmacists; other clinicians and allied health professionals; clinical informaticians; biomedical and clinical engineers; data scientists and AI/ML developers; cybersecurity, privacy, and information technology professionals; human-factors and usability experts; quality and patient-safety leaders; ethicists; regulatory and compliance professionals; healthcare administrators and operational leaders; educators; researchers; and device manufacturers. These stakeholders should be involved throughout the AI lifecycle—from design and validation through implementation, monitoring, reassessment, and retirement—with clearly defined accountability and meaningful human oversight.
